light.notes: Morning sun and afternoon shade suit it best. In deep shade it flowers poorly.

water.notes: Thirsty: water deeply in dry spells. Wilting on a hot afternoon is common; wilting in the morning means it needs water.
water.growingSeason: Water deeply once or twice a week in dry weather; pots daily.

soil.notes: Moist, rich soil. Flower colour follows the soil: blue in acidic soil, pink in alkaline.

toxicity.notes: Contains cyanogenic glycosides. Eating the leaves or flowers can cause vomiting, diarrhoea and lethargy.

guides.feeding: Balanced feed in spring. For blue flowers on neutral soil, use ericaceous feed or a hydrangea colourant.
guides.pruning: Leave old flower heads on over winter to protect the buds, then in early spring cut each back to the first pair of fat buds.

problems.cause: Pruned too hard, or late frost killed the buds
problems.fix: Only cut to the first fat buds in spring, and protect young growth from late frosts.

problems.cause: Dry soil or strong afternoon sun
problems.fix: Water deeply and mulch; move pots into afternoon shade.

problems.symptom: Flowers pink when you wanted blue
problems.fix: Grow in ericaceous compost and water with rainwater.

guides.growthHabit: Rounded deciduous shrub with large mophead or flat lacecap flowers.

water.notes: Water new plants and pots in dry spells; established hedges rarely need it.

toxicity.notes: Contains alkaloids. Eating the leaves causes vomiting and diarrhoea.

guides.pruning: Clip once or twice in early summer, in dry weather.

problems.cause: Box blight, a fungus that spreads in wet weather
problems.fix: Clear fallen leaves, avoid wetting the foliage, clip only in dry weather and remove badly affected plants.

problems.symptom: Webbing and leaves eaten back to the stems
problems.fix: Pick off caterpillars, cut out webbing, and check plants from spring to autumn.

problems.cause: Stress from drought, cold or hunger
problems.fix: Water in dry spells and feed in spring.

guides.growthHabit: Dense evergreen shrub with small leaves; used for hedging and topiary.
guides.matureSize: Kept at any size; unclipped to 5m

light.notes: Full sun for the most flowers; a sunny windowsill indoors.

water.notes: Let the top of the compost dry between waterings. Overwatering causes rot.
water.growingSeason: Pots every few days in hot weather, when the surface is dry.
water.restingSeason: Keep plants overwintering indoors fairly dry.

toxicity.notes: Listed as toxic to cats and dogs. Eating it can cause vomiting and loss of appetite, and contact can irritate skin.

guides.feeding: High-potash feed every 1–2 weeks in summer.
guides.repotting: Pot up overwintered plants in spring.
guides.pruning: Snap off faded flower stalks. Cut back by a third before bringing plants indoors for winter, which they need below 3°C.
guides.propagation: Softwood cuttings root easily in late summer.

problems.fix: Let the compost dry between waterings.
Discard affected plants; take cuttings from healthy stems.
Move into full sun and pinch back.

guides.growthHabit: Bushy tender perennial with rounded, often banded leaves and clusters of flowers.

light.notes: Part shade is ideal; tolerates sun if the soil stays moist.

water.notes: Keep moist in dry spells, especially in its first year.

toxicity.notes: Highly poisonous. All parts contain cardiac glycosides that affect the heart; eating even a small amount can cause vomiting, an irregular heartbeat and death. Wear gloves when handling, and plant away from where children and pets play.

guides.pruning: Cut the main spike after flowering for smaller side spikes, or leave it to self-seed.
guides.propagation: Self-seeds freely; or sow in late spring.

problems.cause: It's a biennial: leaves in year one, flowers in year two
problems.fix: Let some seed fall, or sow every year for a continuous display.
Water the soil in dry spells and improve airflow.

guides.growthHabit: Rosette of soft leaves, then tall spikes of tubular spotted flowers.

water.notes: Water deeply at the base, especially as flower heads form.
water.growingSeason: Deeply once or twice a week in dry weather.
water.restingSeason: It's an annual; it dies after setting seed.

soil.notes: Any well-drained soil; richer soil grows taller plants.

guides.feeding: A general feed every 2 weeks for giant varieties.
guides.pruning: None needed. Leave seed heads for birds, or cover them to harvest.
guides.propagation: Sow seed after the last frost.

problems.fix: Start seeds in pots and plant out once sturdy, with slug protection.
Tie to a strong stake.

guides.growthHabit: Tall annual with large yellow flower heads that follow the sun when young.

light.notes: Dappled shade, sheltered from strong wind and hot afternoon sun.

water.notes: Keep the soil moist in dry spells. Trees in pots dry out quickly.
water.growingSeason: Pots often; ground plants in dry spells.

guides.repotting: Every 2–3 years for trees in containers.
guides.pruning: Minimal. Remove dead or crossing branches while dormant in winter.
guides.propagation: Grafting for named varieties; seed for species.

problems.symptom: Brown, crispy leaf edges in summer
problems.cause: Wind, hot sun or dry soil
problems.fix: Shelter it, water in dry spells and mulch.

problems.symptom: Sudden wilting of a whole branch
problems.fix: Cut back to healthy wood; badly affected trees may need replacing.

guides.growthHabit: Graceful deciduous tree or shrub with deeply lobed leaves and strong autumn colour.

light.notes: Grows almost anywhere with some sun.

water.notes: Needs no watering; its deep taproot finds water.

soil.notes: Any soil, including lawns and cracks in paving.

guides.pruning: To stop it spreading, remove the flowers before they turn into seed clocks.
guides.propagation: Wind-blown seed, and any piece of root left in the ground.

problems.fix: Remove flower heads early, dig out plants with the whole taproot, and thicken the lawn so seedlings can't establish.
Use a narrow weeding tool to lift the whole taproot.

guides.growthHabit: Rosette of toothed leaves from a deep taproot; yellow flowers become round seed clocks. Young leaves are edible.

water.notes: Water pots well in summer; drought-tolerant in the ground once established.
water.growingSeason: Pots several times a week in heat.
water.restingSeason: Keep pots on the dry side in a cool, frost-free place.

toxicity.notes: All parts are highly poisonous, containing cardiac glycosides. Eating even a small amount can be fatal to people and pets. Wear gloves when pruning, and never burn the clippings — the smoke is toxic too.

guides.feeding: High-potash feed every 2 weeks in summer.

problems.fix: Let pots dry a little between waterings and protect from frost.
Move it into full sun.
Wash or wipe them off.

guides.growthHabit: Evergreen shrub with narrow leathery leaves and clusters of pink, red or white flowers.

water.notes: Keep the soil moist, especially in spring.

toxicity.notes: All parts contain cardiac glycosides and are highly poisonous. Eating any part — including the red berries, or water from a vase of cut flowers — can cause vomiting, an irregular heartbeat and death. It isn't a true lily.

guides.feeding: Leaf mould or compost mulch in autumn.
guides.propagation: Divide the rhizomes after flowering or in autumn.

problems.fix: Dig out the edges each year, or plant it with a root barrier.
Normal; water in dry spells to keep it going longer.

guides.growthHabit: Low, spreading carpets of paired leaves with arching stems of scented white bells.

light.notes: Part shade, sheltered from early morning sun, which damages frosted buds.

water.notes: Keep the soil moist with rainwater, especially in late summer when next year's buds form.

guides.feeding: Ericaceous feed in spring and early summer.
guides.repotting: Every 2–3 years for pots, in ericaceous compost.

problems.cause: Dry soil in late summer, when the buds formed
problems.fix: Water consistently from midsummer onwards.

problems.cause: Lime in the soil or water
problems.fix: Use rainwater and ericaceous feed.

problems.cause: Sooty mould on honeydew from scale insects
problems.fix: Treat the scale; the mould washes off.

guides.growthHabit: Evergreen shrub with glossy leaves and rose-like flowers in late winter and spring.

light.notes: Sun or shade; variegated forms colour best in sun.

water.notes: Water young plants until established.

toxicity.notes: Listed as toxic to cats and dogs. The berries cause vomiting and diarrhoea, and the spiny leaves can injure mouths. The berries are also harmful to children.

problems.cause: A male plant, or a female with no male nearby
problems.fix: Only female hollies berry, and they need a male within pollinating distance.
Pick off affected leaves; it rarely harms the plant.

guides.growthHabit: Evergreen shrub or tree with spiny, glossy leaves and red winter berries on female plants.

water.notes: Water young plants until established. It hates waterlogged soil.
water.growingSeason: In dry spells for young plants.

toxicity.notes: Extremely poisonous. The foliage and seeds contain toxins that can cause tremors, seizures and fatal heart failure in pets and people. The red flesh around the seed is the only part that isn't toxic — the seed inside is.

guides.feeding: A general feed in spring for hedges.
guides.pruning: Clip in late summer. Unlike most conifers it regrows from old wood, so it can be cut back hard.

problems.fix: Improve drainage.
Cut back one side per year and feed in spring.

guides.growthHabit: Dense, dark evergreen conifer with red berry-like cones on female plants; long-lived.
guides.matureSize: Kept at any size; unclipped to 15m

light.notes: Sun or part shade outdoors; a bright, cool spot for bulbs forced indoors.

water.notes: Keep moist while growing and flowering; the bulbs rest dry in summer.
water.growingSeason: Let foliage die back naturally, then keep bulbs dry.
water.restingSeason: Keep lightly moist from autumn planting through flowering.

soil.notes: Free-draining soil or compost; bulbs rot in wet soil.

toxicity.notes: Contains alkaloids, concentrated in the bulb. Eating it causes vomiting, diarrhoea and drooling. Handling bulbs can irritate skin — wear gloves.

guides.feeding: A high-potash feed after flowering, while the leaves are green.
guides.pruning: Cut off the flower stalk after flowering; leave the leaves to die down.

problems.cause: Normal for hyacinths after the first year
problems.fix: Plant forced bulbs outdoors after flowering and enjoy looser spikes, or buy fresh bulbs.
Plant in free-draining soil.

guides.growthHabit: Spring bulb with strap leaves and a dense, intensely scented flower spike.

water.notes: Drought-tolerant once established. Water pots when the top few centimetres are dry.

toxicity.notes: Listed as toxic to cats and dogs; eating it can cause vomiting and drooling.

guides.feeding: Balanced feed monthly for pots in summer.
guides.pruning: Pull off old, brown lower leaves. If frost kills the top, cut the stem back to healthy growth in spring; it usually resprouts.

problems.symptom: Top turns brown and mushy after a hard winter
problems.fix: Cut back to healthy growth in late spring and wait for new shoots.
Pull them off.

guides.growthHabit: Palm-like tree with tufts of long, sword-shaped leaves; not a true palm.
guides.matureSize: 1–2m in pots; 5m or more in the ground

water.notes: Let the top of the soil dry between waterings; it rots if kept wet.
water.growingSeason: Water pots when the surface is dry.
water.restingSeason: Usually grown as a summer annual.

toxicity.notes: Contains vinca alkaloids. Eating it can cause vomiting, low blood pressure, tremors and seizures in pets, and it's harmful to people too.

guides.feeding: Balanced feed every 2 weeks in summer.

problems.fix: Water less and improve drainage.
Full sun and pinching.

guides.growthHabit: Compact, glossy-leaved plant with flat five-petalled flowers all summer.

water.notes: Water new hedging until established.
water.growingSeason: In dry spells for the first year.

toxicity.notes: The leaves and seeds contain cyanogenic compounds that release cyanide when chewed or crushed. Keep children away from the berries' seeds, and don't shred or burn clippings in enclosed spaces.

guides.pruning: Trim with secateurs rather than a hedge trimmer, which leaves torn, browning leaves. Late spring or summer.

problems.fix: Remove affected growth; healthy, well-fed plants usually shrug it off.
Improve drainage and water in dry spells.

guides.growthHabit: Fast, dense evergreen shrub with large glossy leaves; widely used for hedging.
guides.matureSize: Kept at any size; unclipped to 8m

water.notes: Needs no care; it thrives on moist, fertile ground.

soil.notes: Rich, disturbed soil high in nitrogen — often a sign of fertile ground.

toxicity.notes: Stinging hairs inject irritants that cause a burning, itchy rash — dogs are often stung on noses and paws. Cooking destroys the sting, and young leaves are edible.

guides.pruning: Cut before it sets seed. It's an important food plant for butterfly caterpillars, so consider leaving a patch.

problems.fix: Wearing gloves, dig out the yellow roots, or cut repeatedly to weaken it.
Wash the area with soap and cool water; dock leaves are folklore, but the cooling can help.

guides.growthHabit: Upright perennial with toothed, hairy leaves on square stems.

light.notes: At least 6 hours of sun a day.

water.notes: Water deeply at the base in dry spells rather than little and often; keep water off the leaves.
water.growingSeason: Deeply once a week in dry weather; pots more often.

soil.notes: Rich, well-drained soil improved with plenty of organic matter.

genusFallbacks.feeding: Rose feed in spring and again after the first flush of flowers.
genusFallbacks.pruning: In late winter, remove dead, damaged and crossing stems, then shorten the rest to an outward-facing bud. Deadhead through summer. Climbers and ramblers are pruned differently.

problems.symptom: Black spots on leaves, which then yellow and fall
problems.fix: Clear fallen leaves, improve airflow, water at the base, and choose resistant varieties.

problems.symptom: White powder on leaves and buds
problems.fix: Water the soil in dry spells and thin crowded growth.

problems.symptom: Clusters of green or pink insects on buds
problems.fix: Squash them, blast them off with water, or leave them for ladybirds.

genusFallbacks.growthHabit: Shrubs, climbers and ramblers with thorny stems and scented flowers. Watch for thorns.

light.notes: Most prefer morning sun and afternoon shade; panicle types take more sun.

water.notes: Thirsty shrubs: water deeply in dry spells.

toxicity.notes: Hydrangeas contain cyanogenic glycosides. Eating them causes vomiting, diarrhoea and lethargy.

genusFallbacks.pruning: Depends on type: mophead and lacecap to the first fat buds in spring; panicle and smooth hydrangeas can be cut harder in late winter.

problems.cause: Wrong pruning for the type, or frost-damaged buds
problems.fix: Check which type you have before pruning.
Water deeply and mulch.

genusFallbacks.growthHabit: Deciduous shrubs and climbers with large flower heads.

water.notes: Water pots and new plants in dry spells.

toxicity.notes: Box contains alkaloids that cause vomiting and diarrhoea if eaten.

genusFallbacks.pruning: Clip in early summer in dry weather.

problems.fix: Clip in dry weather and clear fallen leaves.
Remove caterpillars and webbing.

genusFallbacks.growthHabit: Dense evergreen shrubs for hedging and topiary.

water.notes: Let the compost surface dry between waterings.

toxicity.notes: Pelargoniums are listed as toxic to cats and dogs: vomiting, loss of appetite and skin irritation.

genusFallbacks.feeding: High-potash feed every 1–2 weeks in summer.
genusFallbacks.pruning: Deadhead; cut back before overwintering indoors.

problems.fix: Let it dry between waterings.
Take cuttings from healthy growth.

genusFallbacks.growthHabit: Tender perennials: zonal, ivy-leaved, regal and scented-leaf types.

water.notes: Keep the compost moist in summer; baskets can need water daily.
water.restingSeason: Keep tender types barely moist and frost-free.

genusFallbacks.feeding: High-potash feed every 1–2 weeks in summer.
genusFallbacks.pruning: Hardy types: cut back in spring. Tender types: trim before overwintering.

problems.fix: Water regularly and give it some shade.
Cut off affected shoots and bin them.

genusFallbacks.growthHabit: Shrubs with dangling, two-coloured flowers; hardy and tender types.

water.notes: Bulbs need little water; they rot in wet soil.
water.growingSeason: Let the leaves die down after flowering; keep bulbs dry in summer.
water.restingSeason: Rain is enough; water pots occasionally in spring growth.

soil.notes: Free-draining soil. Plant bulbs in late autumn, three times their depth.

toxicity.notes: The bulbs are most toxic. Eating them causes vomiting, diarrhoea and drooling; handling bulbs can cause a skin rash ('tulip fingers').

genusFallbacks.feeding: High-potash feed after flowering if keeping bulbs.
genusFallbacks.pruning: Deadhead after flowering; leave the leaves for 6 weeks.

problems.cause: Many hybrids decline after the first year
problems.fix: Plant deeper, or treat showy varieties as annuals.

problems.symptom: Twisted, spotted leaves and grey mould
problems.fix: Remove and bin affected plants; plant new bulbs elsewhere.

water.notes: Water in dry spring weather while in growth.
water.growingSeason: Leave the foliage to die down for about 6 weeks after flowering.

soil.notes: Free-draining soil. Plant bulbs in early autumn, two to three times their depth.

toxicity.notes: Contains lycorine, concentrated in the bulb. Eating it causes vomiting, drooling and diarrhoea. People have been poisoned by mistaking bulbs for onions. The sap can irritate skin.

genusFallbacks.pruning: Deadhead, but don't cut or knot the leaves until they yellow.
genusFallbacks.propagation: Lift and divide crowded clumps after the leaves die down.

problems.cause: Crowded clumps, or leaves cut too soon last year
problems.fix: Divide the clump and let the foliage die back naturally.
Improve drainage; discard soft bulbs.

light.notes: Shade or part shade; blue-leaved kinds keep their colour best in shade.

water.notes: Keep the soil moist, especially in pots.

toxicity.notes: Contains saponins. Eating it causes vomiting and diarrhoea in pets.

genusFallbacks.pruning: Remove flower stalks and dead leaves in autumn.

problems.fix: Protect new shoots early in spring; grow in pots with copper tape, or choose thick-leaved varieties.
Move into shade.

genusFallbacks.growthHabit: Clump-forming perennials grown for bold leaves.

light.notes: Dappled or part shade; dwarf types take more sun.

water.notes: Shallow roots dry out quickly. Water with rainwater in dry spells, especially in late summer when buds form.
water.growingSeason: Regularly in dry weather; pots often.

soil.notes: Acidic, ericaceous, humus-rich soil. Mulch to keep roots cool.

toxicity.notes: All parts contain grayanotoxins. Eating even a few leaves can cause vomiting, drooling, weakness, low blood pressure and heart problems in pets. Honey made from the flowers has poisoned people.

genusFallbacks.pruning: Deadhead after flowering; prune lightly then if needed.

problems.fix: Water with rainwater and use ericaceous feed with iron.

problems.symptom: Buds turning brown and failing to open
problems.cause: Dry late summer, or bud blast fungus
problems.fix: Water in late summer and remove affected buds.

genusFallbacks.growthHabit: Evergreen or deciduous shrubs with clusters of showy flowers.

light.notes: Flowers in the sun, with roots shaded by other plants or a tile.

water.notes: Water deeply in dry spells, especially in the first few years.

soil.notes: Rich, moist, well-drained soil. Plant 5–8cm deeper than it was in its pot.

toxicity.notes: Contains irritant compounds. Eating it causes drooling, vomiting and diarrhoea; the sap can blister skin.

genusFallbacks.feeding: High-potash feed in spring and summer.
genusFallbacks.pruning: Depends on its pruning group: early-flowering types after flowering; large-flowered types lightly in late winter; late-flowering types cut hard to 30cm in late winter.

problems.fix: Cut back to healthy growth, even below ground; deep planting helps it regrow.
Check its group and prune at the right time.

genusFallbacks.growthHabit: Climbers that twine by their leaf stalks.

water.notes: Water young plants until established.

toxicity.notes: Holly berries cause vomiting and diarrhoea, and spiny leaves can injure mouths. The berries are also harmful to children.

problems.cause: Male plant, or no male nearby
problems.fix: Plant a male holly nearby.
Remove affected leaves.

genusFallbacks.growthHabit: Evergreen or deciduous shrubs and trees.

water.notes: Water young plants; never waterlogged.

toxicity.notes: Yews are extremely poisonous. Foliage and seeds can cause seizures and fatal heart failure in pets and people.

genusFallbacks.pruning: Clip in late summer; regrows from old wood.

problems.fix: Improve drainage.
Cut back in stages and feed.

light.notes: Flowers in the sun, with the base and roots shaded.

water.notes: Keep moist while growing; the bulbs rot in waterlogged soil.
water.growingSeason: Water regularly in dry weather; pots often.
water.restingSeason: Keep pots barely moist over winter.

toxicity.notes: Deadly to cats. Every part — petals, leaves, pollen, even water from the vase — can cause kidney failure within days, and a cat that licks pollen off its fur is at risk. Get to a vet immediately, even if the cat seems well. Not listed as toxic to dogs.

genusFallbacks.feeding: High-potash feed every 2 weeks from shoots appearing until flowering ends.
genusFallbacks.pruning: Remove faded flowers; leave the stem until it yellows.

problems.symptom: Bright red beetles and holes in leaves
problems.fix: Pick off beetles and the sticky larvae under the leaves from spring onwards.
Plant on a layer of grit, or in pots.

genusFallbacks.growthHabit: Bulbs with tall leafy stems and large trumpet or turk's-cap flowers.

light.notes: Full sun for the most flowers.

water.notes: Drought-tolerant once established; water in long dry spells for better flowering.

soil.notes: Almost any soil that isn't waterlogged.

toxicity.notes: Deadly to cats: like true lilies, every part can cause kidney failure within days. Get to a vet immediately if a cat eats any. Not listed as toxic to dogs.

genusFallbacks.pruning: Remove faded flower stalks and tidy dead leaves in autumn.

problems.fix: Divide in spring and give it more sun.

problems.symptom: Swollen buds that fail to open
problems.fix: Pick off and bin swollen buds.

genusFallbacks.growthHabit: Clumps of arching leaves with trumpet flowers that each last a day.

light.notes: Most want full sun; some grow in damp shade.

water.notes: Bearded irises like it dry; moisture-loving kinds need wet soil. Know which you have.

soil.notes: Bearded irises: well-drained, with rhizomes sitting on the surface. Water irises: boggy soil.

toxicity.notes: Irises contain irritant compounds, concentrated in the rhizomes and bulbs. Eating them causes drooling, vomiting and diarrhoea; the sap can irritate skin.

genusFallbacks.pruning: Cut flowered stems to the base; trim leaves into fans in late summer.

problems.cause: Crowded rhizomes, or buried too deep
problems.fix: Divide and replant with rhizomes on the surface.
Remove affected leaves and improve airflow.

genusFallbacks.growthHabit: Sword-shaped leaves with distinctive flowers, from rhizomes or bulbs.

water.notes: Keep moist while growing.
water.restingSeason: Garden ranunculus corms rest dry after flowering.

toxicity.notes: Buttercups contain protoanemonin, which irritates the mouth and gut and can blister skin. Grazing animals avoid them when fresh.

genusFallbacks.pruning: Deadhead garden types; remove weedy buttercups before they spread.

problems.symptom: Creeping buttercup taking over beds or lawn
problems.fix: Dig out plants with their roots, and improve drainage in damp lawns.
Lift and store corms dry.

genusFallbacks.growthHabit: From creeping weeds to showy corms with layered, rose-like flowers.

light.notes: Part shade, out of early morning sun.

water.notes: Keep moist with rainwater, especially in late summer.

problems.fix: Water consistently from midsummer.
Rainwater and ericaceous feed.

genusFallbacks.growthHabit: Evergreen shrubs with glossy leaves; includes the tea plant.

water.notes: Keep moist in dry spells.

toxicity.notes: Foxgloves contain cardiac glycosides. Eating any part can cause vomiting, an irregular heartbeat and death. Wear gloves when handling.

genusFallbacks.pruning: Cut spent spikes, or leave to self-seed.

problems.fix: Let it self-seed.
Water in dry spells.

genusFallbacks.growthHabit: Rosettes followed by tall flower spikes.

water.notes: Water deeply at the base in dry spells.
water.restingSeason: Annuals die after seeding; perennials die back.

genusFallbacks.pruning: Stake tall plants; cut perennials down in autumn.

problems.fix: Start in pots and protect.
Stake.

genusFallbacks.growthHabit: Annuals and perennials with daisy-like yellow flowers.
